clue.text: American river and Babylonian city, that was Rome

definitions.note: completes Poe's line about Rome; the answer is the noun missing before it

blocks.note: the Rio Grande, on the US-Mexico border, often called just the Grande
Ur of the Chaldees, the ancient Mesopotamian city

explanation.surface: A tourist's trivia list pairing an American river and an ancient city with the Rome of old.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a quotation: Edgar Allan Poe wrote of 'the glory that was Greece, and the grandeur that was Rome'.
explanation.definitionFit: Poe's famous line pairs Greek glory with Roman magnificence, so the missing word is the quality that ancient Rome possessed.

clue.text: Wordsworth's birth was dead to the world

blocks.note: Wordsworth's Immortality Ode says 'Our birth is but a sleep and a forgetting'
idiom for being deeply unconscious in slumber

explanation.surface: A grim-sounding remark that the poet's birth left him dead to the world.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half needs the line from Wordsworth's Ode: 'Our birth is but a sleep and a forgetting', so his birth was 'a sleep', read as one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone dead to the world is in deep slumber, which is exactly the state of being not awake.

clue.text: He created the 14 11 and she 8

blocks.note: Samuel, the Lancashire inventor of the spinning mule for cotton in 1779
Richmal, the author of the Just William children's books

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves rest on cross-references: 14 and 11 together give SPINNING MULE, and 8 gives JUST WILLIAM. One surname belongs to an inventor and to a woman author.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel the Lancashire inventor and Richmal the author of the schoolboy stories happen to share the same family name.

clue.text: Musical note on top of soprano?

definitions.note: describes the answer by where it sits, rather than naming it

blocks.note: the 1960s hippie stage show
the first note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Asks which musical note sits above the soprano line in a score.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Musical note' reads as one phrase, but splits into a named show and a sol-fa note. The question mark flags the playful definition: what sits on a singer's head.
explanation.definitionFit: A styled arrangement of hair is literally worn on the head of a soprano singer, so it sits on top of her.

clue.text: The front way to Nottingham?

definitions.note: the answer is the word that follows Nottingham in its football club's name

blocks.note: fore means the front part
St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: Directions asking for the main road into Nottingham.
explanation.walkthrough: Nottingham Forest is the city's football club, and nearby Sherwood Forest is Robin Hood's home, which 19 down picks up.
explanation.definitionFit: Nottingham Forest is the famous English football club, so this word completes the city's name in the team's title.

clue.text: ... of note: one was a dog, in lieu of a mouse

indicators.note: read as 'in the place', telling the solver the answer sits in place inside the words that follow

blocks.note: surface padding: a hint at Enid Blyton's gang of four children and Timmy the dog
the letters run across the three words, dropping the first O and the final E

explanation.surface: Continues the previous clue, musing on a celebrated gang in which a dog stood in for a mouse.
explanation.walkthrough: The dog is Timmy of Enid Blyton's Famous Five, a hint at the answer; the letters themselves are hidden in 'of a mouse'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being of note means being well known and celebrated, a straightforward adjective synonym for renowned.

clue.text: It isn't played in school

blocks.note: surface reading: a game that is banned from the school playground
setter's reading: someone who has 'played' hooky, and so is not in school at all

explanation.walkthrough: 'Played' looks like games; the idiom is 'play truant', and the one who does so is absent from school.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil who skips lessons without permission is said to play hooky, and is thus not present at school.

clue.text: Model waitresses harassed by 17

blocks.note: the Model T, Ford's early car
Hebe was cupbearer to the Greek gods, so hebes are waitresses

explanation.surface: Waitresses in a model restaurant being pestered by an awkward customer.
explanation.walkthrough: 17 is SPHINX: in Greek myth the Sphinx sat outside the city and devoured any traveller who failed her riddle until Oedipus solved it.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek city in Boeotia was terrorised by the riddling monster of myth, which Oedipus eventually defeated.

clue.text: Fair morning: do I intend to enter 18 of the 19s?

definitions.note: a book title, defined as the stories of a gang

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so one piece goes inside the other two joined

blocks.note: fair and just are synonyms
'will I' asks whether I intend
a.m., ante meridiem

explanation.surface: Someone wondering on a fine morning whether they mean to go in.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 is CHRONICLES and 19 is OUTLAW: William Brown and his friends called themselves the Outlaws in Richmal Crompton's books.
explanation.definitionFit: Crompton's books recount the escapades of William and his gang the Outlaws, so the series chronicles that gang.

clue.text: Cutting short a geneticist is fine and probably honorable

definitions.note: the answer is a fine, usually found in the French phrase with honorable

indicators.note: cutting something short trims off its end

blocks.note: taken as written
Gregor Mendel, father of genetics

explanation.surface: Sounds like a censor trimming a scientist and declaring it fine and honourable.
explanation.walkthrough: The French 'amende honorable' is a public apology, so 'probably honorable' nods to the word that usually follows; on its own the answer means a fine.
explanation.definitionFit: In French and in legal English the word means a penalty or reparation, most often met in the phrase 'amende honorable'.

clue.text: Immaculate, which is an advantage on the field

definitions.note: describes the state rather than naming it

blocks.note: spotless, without a blemish
a footballer with no opponent guarding him is free to receive the ball

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is from football: a player not closely guarded by a defender is free for a pass.
explanation.definitionFit: Spotless means without stains or blemishes, and in team sports a player left free by defenders is in a good position.

clue.text: What's afoot? A 23

blocks.note: read literally: what is worn on a foot, a backless slipper
23 is HYBRID: the offspring of a donkey and a horse

explanation.walkthrough: 'What's afoot?' normally asks what is happening; here it asks what is on a foot.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a backless slipper and the sterile offspring of a male donkey and a mare.

clue.text: Little one, the one on the right, he's asking for it

blocks.note: French for small
Roman numeral one
taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Pointing out a small child on the right who is plainly asking for trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Asking for it' usually means courting trouble; here it is literal, one who makes a formal request.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who presents a formal written request, as to a court or authority, is literally asking for something.

clue.text: A minister's a trained servant of the state on this view

definitions.text: servant of the state on this view
definitions.note: describes the doctrine by what it makes the church

indicators.note: something trained has been reshaped, so these letters are reworked

blocks.note: every letter of these words is used

explanation.surface: Says a church minister is merely a trained civil servant.
explanation.walkthrough: The doctrine is named after Thomas Erastus, who held that the state should have authority over the church; the whole clue reads as a summary of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Erastus's doctrine subordinates church to civil power, so under it a clergyman is in effect an employee of government.

clue.text: Top job in politics?

blocks.note: surface reading: the highest post in government, such as prime minister
setter's reading: what a top does, and the job of a press officer putting a gloss on news

explanation.walkthrough: 'Top job' looks like the premiership; it is the action of a toy top, and also 'spin', a press officer's twisting of the news.
explanation.definitionFit: A toy top rotates rapidly, and political media advisers are known as spin doctors for presenting stories favourably.

clue.text: Butt originating with the head of a pig?

definitions.text: with the head of a pig?

blocks.note: a cigarette butt is its stub
something born has its origin

explanation.surface: Wonders whether a butt comes from a pig's head, as in a cut of pork.
explanation.walkthrough: Pig-headed means obstinate; the question mark admits the literal reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A pig-headed person is obstinate and refuses to change their mind, so the idiom is taken literally here.

clue.text: Whereas there's a sort of drive for a learner to enter

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so one letter is placed within the other word

blocks.note: a whist drive is a social evening of card games
L for learner, as on L-plates

explanation.surface: Contrasts drivers, noting a learner is about to set off.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'drive' here is not motoring: a whist drive is a British social evening of whist, a card game, so the learner suggests L-plates falsely.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words introduce a contrast between two statements, as conjunctions meaning 'while on the other hand'.

clue.text: Enigmatist jumping ship at New Cross?

indicators.note: things that jump move about, so the letters are thrown into new order

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new
X is a cross

explanation.surface: A puzzle setter deserting ship at New Cross, a district of south-east London.
explanation.walkthrough: New Cross looks like a place in London, but splits into two abbreviations. The answer is the riddling monster of Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical creature posed a famous riddle to travellers, so it is the original setter of puzzles.

clue.text: Bible stories of a very bad little boy

blocks.note: informal British usage: chronic means dreadful
Les is a short form of the boy's name Leslie

explanation.surface: Bible stories told about a very naughty child.
explanation.walkthrough: In informal British English 'chronic' means very bad, not just long-lasting. 'Little' signals a shortened name.
explanation.definitionFit: Two books of the Old Testament carry this name, recounting the history of the kings of Judah.

clue.text: Opposite of spouse's relation living in 5 across?

definitions.note: describes by a typical home; Robin Hood lived in Sherwood

indicators.note: taking the opposite swaps a word part for its antonym

blocks.note: a relative by marriage

explanation.surface: A family joke about the in-laws who live out in the woods.
explanation.walkthrough: IN becomes its opposite OUT. 5 across is FOREST: the bandit Robin Hood lived in Sherwood Forest.
explanation.definitionFit: Robin Hood, the most famous bandit of English legend, made his home in Sherwood with his merry men.

clue.text: Things are said to have one, namely a male setter

definitions.text: Things are said to have one

blocks.note: sc. is short for scilicet, Latin for 'namely'
he is a male pronoun
the setter refers to themself as me

explanation.surface: Things, we are told, each have a male setter.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition rests on the phrase 'the scheme of things', the overall plan in which everything has its place.
explanation.definitionFit: People speak of 'the scheme of things', so things are proverbially said to have an underlying plan.

clue.text: Turn of speed? That's as may be

blocks.note: a variant spelling of oomph, energy or zip
a sceptical grunt like 'humph', expressing doubt

explanation.walkthrough: The word is both a spelling of 'oomph', vigour, and an interjection of grudging doubt.
explanation.definitionFit: Oomph is vigorous energy, and a doubtful grunt conveys the same reservation as the phrase 'that's as may be'.

clue.text: The original 20 about sunburn was used as a pregnancy test

definitions.text: was used as a pregnancy test
definitions.note: describes the creature by its former use

indicators.note: about means around, so one word wraps the other

blocks.note: 20 is SCHEME; the original one is Plan A
a tan is skin darkened by sun

explanation.surface: An old scheme for sunburn once doubled as a pregnancy test.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the African clawed frog, Xenopus: injected with a woman's urine, it laid eggs if she was pregnant.
explanation.definitionFit: The South African clawed frog was widely used in mid-century hospital laboratories as a living test for pregnancy.

clue.text: Hear a call for some bridges to cross

indicators.note: hearing means taking the word by its sound, not its spelling
only some of the word is wanted, so its end is dropped

blocks.note: a greeting called out
taken as written, then trimmed

explanation.surface: Calling out to someone across a set of bridges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like a verb going with bridges; it is the noun, a mix of breeds.
explanation.definitionFit: A cross is the offspring of two different breeds or species, the same thing as a crossbred organism.

clue.text: Girl in test for radio

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the name goes within the other word

blocks.note: a try is an attempt or test
a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl being auditioned for a radio part.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is dated British slang for a transistor radio.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for transistor, it was everyday British slang in the 1960s and 70s for a portable wireless set.

clue.text: Tile with no T, vocal quality unknown

indicators.note: having none of a letter means taking it out

blocks.note: the letter to be removed
timbre is the tone colour of a voice
x is the algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A tile missing a T, and a voice of unknown quality: two items from an odd list.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a curved Roman roof tile laid over the joints of flat tiles.
explanation.definitionFit: In classical architecture this was the curved roofing piece covering the gap between two flat tiles.
